module_title: Soil Preparation and Fertility for Herbal Plants

lessons.title: Testing Your Soil: Simple pH and Texture Tests for African Soils
lessons.body:
Before you plant any medicinal herb, you need to know what kind of soil you have. Two quick testsâpH and textureâwill tell you most of what you need. For pH, you can use a simple vinegar and baking soda test. Take a handful of soil, put it in a cup, add a few drops of vinegar. If it fizzes, your soil is alkaline (pH above 7). If no fizz, take another sample, add water to make mud, then add baking soda. If it fizzes, your soil is acidic (pH below 7). No fizz either time means your soil is roughly neutral (pH 6.5â7.5), which is ideal for most herbs. For a more precise reading, buy a cheap pH test kit from an agroâdealer; they cost about 5,000â10,000 shillings and give a color chart.

Texture is about how much sand, silt, and clay your soil has. Do a jar test: fill a clear jar oneâthird with soil, top up with water, add a pinch of salt, shake hard for 3 minutes, then let it settle for 24 hours. Sand settles first (bottom layer), then silt, then clay on top. Measure each layer as a percentage. If sand is over 70%, your soil is sandyâit drains fast but loses nutrients. If clay is over 40%, itâs heavy clayâholds water but roots can rot. The best for herbs is loam: roughly 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay. In many African soils, youâll find sandy loam or clay loam. Knowing this tells you how to amend: sandy soil needs compost and mulch; clay soil needs sand, compost, and raised beds.

Also check for earthworms. Dig a 30 cm x 30 cm hole, count worms. If you find 10 or more, your soil is alive and fertile. Fewer than 3 means you need to add organic matter. Do these tests before preparing beds. Write down your results. For example, if your pH is 5.5 (acidic) and texture is sandy loam, youâll need to add wood ash or lime to raise pH, plus plenty of compost. If pH is 8.0 (alkaline), add compost, manure, or sulfur. These simple tests cost almost nothing and save you from crop failure.

lessons.title: Making Compost from Local Materials: Kitchen Waste, Manure, and Crop Residues
lessons.body:
Compost is the cheapest and best fertilizer for herbal plants. You can make it from things you already have: kitchen scraps (vegetable peels, eggshells, tea leaves), animal manure (cow, goat, chicken, rabbit), and crop residues (maize stalks, bean haulms, banana leaves, grass clippings). The goal is to create a pile that heats up to 55â65Â°C, which kills weed seeds and pathogens. Start by choosing a shaded spot near your garden. Clear a 1.5 m x 1.5 m area. Put down a 15 cm layer of coarse material like maize stalks or twigs for airflow.

Now build your pile in layers. A good recipe: 3 parts brown (dry, carbonârich) to 1 part green (wet, nitrogenârich) by volume. Brown materials: dry leaves, straw, maize cobs, sawdust (use sparingly). Green materials: fresh grass, kitchen waste, manure, green leaves. For every 30 cm of brown, add 10 cm of green. Sprinkle water as you goâthe pile should be as wet as a squeezed sponge. Add a handful of wood ash or a little topsoil between layers to introduce microbes. Keep the pile no higher than 1.5 m. Turn it every 2 weeks with a fork or shovel. If it smells bad (like rotten eggs), itâs too wetâadd dry material and turn. If itâs not heating up, itâs too dry or lacks nitrogenâadd water and green material.

In hot African climates, compost can be ready in 6â8 weeks. Itâs done when itâs dark, crumbly, and smells like earth. You should not recognize the original materials. Use it as a 5 cm top dressing around your herbs, or mix it into planting holes at 1 part compost to 2 parts soil. For a 10 mÂ² bed, you need about 100â200 kg of compost per year. One pile of 1.5 m x 1.5 m x 1.5 m can produce 500â800 kg. Thatâs enough for several beds. Never use fresh manure directlyâit burns roots. Compost it first. Also avoid meat, bones, oily foods, and diseased plants. With consistent effort, youâll build soil fertility for free.

lessons.title: Creating Raised Beds and Sunken Beds for Different Climates
lessons.body:
The type of bed you build depends on your climate and soil. In areas with heavy rainfall or poor drainage, use raised beds. In dry areas with little rain, use sunken beds. Raised beds are 20â30 cm high, 1 m wide, and any length. They warm up faster in the morning, drain excess water, and make harvesting easier. Build them by digging soil from the paths between beds and piling it on the bed. Mix in compost and sand if your soil is clay. The paths should be 30â40 cm wide. For a 1 m x 3 m bed, you need about 0.6 cubic meters of soil. Line the sides with stones, wood, or grass to prevent erosion. Raised beds are ideal for herbs like basil, mint, and rosemary in highârainfall areas like the Congo Basin or the Ethiopian highlands.

Sunken beds are the opposite: dig 20â30 cm deep, 1 m wide, and any length. The soil you remove is used to make a small ridge around the bed. Sunken beds catch and hold rainwater, keeping roots moist for longer. They also protect plants from hot dry winds. This is perfect for dry regions like the Sahel, Kalahari, or northern Kenya. Fill the sunken bed with a mix of soil, compost, and manure. Plant your herbs on the flat bottom. The ridges should be 10â15 cm high. In very hot areas, you can mulch the ridges to reduce evaporation. For a 1 m x 3 m sunken bed, youâll need to dig out about 0.6 cubic meters of soil. Thatâs a lot of work, but it pays off in water savings.

In moderate climates, you can use flat bedsâjust loosen the soil to 30 cm depth and add compost. No need for raised or sunken. Whichever bed you choose, always add organic matter. For raised beds in wet areas, mix in 2 buckets of compost per square meter. For sunken beds in dry areas, mix in 3 buckets of compost and 1 bucket of manure per square meter. Test your bed after a heavy rain: if water stands for more than 2 hours, raise it more; if it dries out in a day, sink it. Observe and adjust.

lessons.title: Using Mulch to Conserve Water and Suppress Weeds in Dry Regions
lessons.body:
Mulch is any material you spread on the soil surface. In dry regions, itâs a lifesaver. A good 5â10 cm layer of mulch can reduce evaporation by 50â70%, keep soil temperature cooler, and suppress weeds. For herbal plants, mulch also keeps leaves clean and reduces disease. Use local materials: dry grass, straw, maize stalks, banana leaves, cocoa pods, coffee husks, sawdust (only aged), wood chips, or even stones. Avoid fresh grass clippings that mat down and rotâlet them dry first. Also avoid mulch from diseased plants. In dry areas like the Sahel, you can use crop residues after harvest. For example, after harvesting maize, chop the stalks into 20â30 cm pieces and spread them around your herbs.

How to apply mulch: First, water your plants well. Then spread a layer 5â10 cm thick around the base of each plant, leaving a 2â3 cm gap around the stem to prevent rot. Do not pile mulch against the stem. For a 10 mÂ² bed, you need about 1â2 cubic meters of loose mulch. Thatâs roughly 10â20 wheelbarrows. Reapply as it decomposesâusually every 3â6 months. In very hot, windy areas, you may need to anchor mulch with a few stones or branches. You can also use living mulch: plant lowâgrowing legumes like cowpea or groundnut between your herbs. They cover the soil and fix nitrogen. But keep them trimmed so they donât compete.

Mulch also builds soil organic matter as it breaks down. Earthworms pull it into the soil, improving structure. In dry regions, mulch can mean the difference between life and death for your herbs. For example, in northern Nigeria, farmers who mulch with millet straw grow mint and lemongrass successfully even with only 400 mm of rain per year. Without mulch, those plants would wilt. So collect all your crop residues and use them. Never burn them. Mulch is free and effective. Start today.

lessons.title: Natural Fertilizers: Preparing Manure Tea and Liquid Organic Fertilizers
lessons.body:
Liquid fertilizers give your herbs a quick boost. Manure tea is the easiest. Fill a sack (burlap or woven polypropylene) with 10 kg of fresh animal manureâcow, goat, chicken, or rabbit. Tie the sack and place it in a 200âliter drum filled with water. Let it steep for 3â7 days, stirring daily. The water will turn dark brown. Remove the sack. Dilute the tea with water at 1 part tea to 3 parts water. Apply to your herbs every 2 weeks. For a 10 mÂ² bed, use 5â10 liters of diluted tea. You can also use the soaked manure as compost. Chicken manure is strongestâuse 5 kg per 200 L and dilute 1:5. Never apply undiluted manure tea; it can burn leaves.

You can make liquid fertilizer from other local materials. For example, comfrey or nettle tea: chop 1 kg of fresh comfrey leaves or nettle, add to 10 L of water, let sit for 2â4 weeks. Dilute 1:10. This is rich in potassium and nitrogen. Another recipe: wood ash tea. Mix 1 cup of wood ash in 10 L of water, let sit for 2 days, then use undiluted. This adds potassium and raises pH slightly. For a phosphorus boost, use bone meal tea: crush 1 kg of bones (from butcher), boil, then soak in 10 L water for a week. Dilute 1:5. Banana peels also work: soak 1 kg of chopped peels in 5 L water for 3 days, then dilute 1:2. This provides potassium.

Apply liquid fertilizers to the soil around the plant, not on the leaves, unless youâre foliar feeding. For foliar feeding, strain the tea and spray in the early morning or evening. Always test on a small area first. Store manure tea in a covered container away from children and animals. Use within 2 weeks. These natural fertilizers are cheap and effective. They wonât give instant results like chemical fertilizers, but they build soil health over time. For best results, combine with compost and mulch.

lessons.title: Crop Rotation and Intercropping with Legumes for Soil Health
lessons.body:
Crop rotation means changing what you plant in a bed each season. This prevents pests and diseases from building up, and it balances soil nutrients. Different herbs take different nutrients. For example, leafy herbs like basil and mint need lots of nitrogen. Root herbs like ginger and turmeric need potassium and phosphorus. If you plant the same herb in the same spot year after year, youâll deplete specific nutrients and attract pests. A simple rotation for African gardens: Season 1 â leafy herbs (basil, mint, lemon balm). Season 2 â root herbs (ginger, turmeric, garlic). Season 3 â legumes (cowpea, groundnut, lablab). Season 4 â fruiting herbs (chili, fennel). Then repeat. Legumes fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, so they recharge your beds.

Intercropping is growing two or more crops together. Legumes are perfect companions for herbs. Plant cowpea, groundnut, or lablab between your herb rows. They shade the soil, suppress weeds, and add nitrogen. For example, plant basil with cowpea. The cowpea grows tall and fixes nitrogen; the basil grows bushy and uses that nitrogen. You can also plant lemongrass with groundnutâthe groundnut covers the ground. In dry areas, use droughtâtolerant legumes like cowpea or pigeon pea. In wet areas, use lablab or velvet bean. Space them 30â50 cm apart. Donât intercrop with tall cereals like maizeâthey compete too much.

A good rotation plan for a 3âbed garden: Bed 1: Season 1 â basil + cowpea intercrop; Season 2 â turmeric; Season 3 â groundnut. Bed 2: Season 1 â mint + lablab; Season 2 â ginger; Season 3 â cowpea. Bed 3: Season 1 â lemon balm + groundnut; Season 2 â garlic; Season 3 â pigeon pea. After legumes, plant heavy feeders. Always add compost before each season. This system keeps soil healthy without expensive fertilizers. It also reduces pest problems. For example, marigold (a herb) intercropped with tomato repels nematodes. So use rotation and intercropping as your first line of defense against soil problems.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Soil Preparation and Fertility for Medicinal & Herbal Plants

This reference consolidates the operational essentials from the module. Treat it as a field manual: each section gives you a decision, the numbers behind it, and the input cost or yield implication. For African smallholder and emerging commercial herbal producers, soil is the single largest controllable driver of leaf quality, oil content, and root biomass â and therefore of the price you can ask from buyers, processors, and exporters.

1. Testing Your Soil: pH and Texture

Before you spend money on inputs, spend two hours on a test. Most herbal species tolerate pH 5.5â7.0, but the range narrows for high-value crops. Use a simple field kit (litmus or inexpensive digital pH meter) plus the "jar test" for texture.

Jar test method: Fill a clear jar one-third with soil, top with water, add a pinch of salt, shake hard for 3 minutes, then let settle 24 hours. Sand settles first, then silt, then clay. Measure each layer as a percentage of total.

Table 1. Soil pH and texture targets for selected African-grown medicinal & herbal crops
Crop Ideal pH Preferred texture Business note
Aloe vera6.0â7.0Sandy loam, well-drainedWaterlogging kills roots; raised beds in humid zones
Artemisia annua6.0â7.5LoamHigher artemisinin content on well-drained loam
Moringa oleifera6.3â7.0Sandy loam to loamTolerates poor soils; responds strongly to manure
Hibiscus sabdariffa6.0â6.8Loamy, high organic matterAcid soils reduce calyx yield
Ocimum (basil) spp.6.0â7.0Loam, free-drainingOil content falls on waterlogged clay
Mondia whitei5.5â6.5Humus-rich loamForest species; needs shade and organic matter

Sources: FAO, Soils for Nutrition: State of the Art (2022); IITA, Soil Fertility Management for African Smallholders (2015); Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) crop guides.

2. Composting from Local Materials

Compost is your cheapest fertility input. The rule is roughly 25â30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen by weight. In practice: 3 parts dry crop residue or dry grass to 1 part fresh kitchen waste or manure. Turn every 7â14 days; keep moisture at the "squeezed sponge" level. Ready in 6â10 weeks.

Table 2. Approximate nutrient content of common African farmyard inputs (dry-weight basis)
Material N (%) P (%) K (%) Practical note
Cattle manure (fresh)0.4â0.60.2â0.30.4â0.6Best composted before use
Poultry litter1.5â3.00.8â1.50.8â1.5High N; dilute in manure tea
Goat manure0.8â1.20.4â0.60.8â1.0Good all-round amendment
Composted kitchen waste0.5â1.00.2â0.50.5â1.0Watch for salt and plastics
Legume crop residue (beans)1.5â2.50.2â0.41.0â2.0Fixes N in rotation

Sources: FAO, Plant Nutrition for Food Security (Rome, 2006), Table 3.4; IITA, Integrated Soil Fertility Management training materials (2015); KALRO soil fertility bulletins.

3. Raised vs. Sunken Beds

Raised beds (30â40 cm high): use in humid and high-rainfall zones â coastal Kenya, Uganda, southern Nigeria, Cameroon. They prevent waterlogging, improve aeration, and reduce root rot in aloe, basil, and Artemisia.

Sunken beds (15â25 cm deep): use in semi-arid and dry zones â northern Kenya, Sahel, Botswana, Namibia. The zai pit system captures runoff and concentrates compost and manure at the root zone, boosting yields on degraded soils.

4. Mulching for Dry Regions

Apply 5â10 cm of organic mulch (dry grass, straw, crop residue, chopped maize stalks) around plants, keeping a 5 cm gap from stems. Benefits: 30â50% reduction in evaporation, weed suppression, and gradual nutrient release as mulch decomposes. In dryland Africa, mulching is often the single highest-return soil intervention per hour of labour.

5. Natural Fertilizers: Manure Tea and Liquid Organic Fertilizers

Manure tea: Place 1 part well-rotted manure in a porous sack, submerge in 10 parts water in a drum, steep 3â7 days, stirring daily. Dilute 1:1 with water before applying. Use as a foliar spray or soil drench every 2 weeks.

Liquid organic fertilizer (LOF): Ferment chopped green matter (comfrey, tithonia, banana pseudostem) in water for 10â14 days. Rich in potassium and micronutrients. Ideal for leafy herbs and fruiting crops.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Manure and Compost Handling

Raw manure and manure tea can carry E. coli, Salmonella, and parasitic eggs. Always: (1) compost manure for at least 60 days at 55â65 Â°C before use on edible herbs; (2) wear gloves and boots when handling; (3) never apply raw manure tea within 90 days of harvest on crops eaten fresh; (4) wash hands and tools after handling; (5) do not use human waste or manure from sick animals. If selling to processors or exporters, keep records of compost dates â buyers increasingly audit this.

6. Crop Rotation and Intercropping with Legumes

Rotate herbal crops with legumes (beans, cowpea, groundnut, lablab) to break pest cycles and fix nitrogen. A practical 3-season rotation for a 1-acre herbal plot:

  • Season 1: Legume (cowpea or groundnut) â fixes 40â80 kg N/ha.
  • Season 2: Heavy-feeding herb (Artemisia, Hibiscus) â exploits residual N.
  • Season 3: Light-feeding herb (Aloe, basil) or fallow with compost.

Intercropping herbs with legumes (e.g., basil + cowpea) increases total land productivity by 20â40% and reduces fertilizer needs. This is the business case: lower input cost per kg of dried herb.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test pH and texture before planting â record results in a field notebook.
  2. Build compost with a 3:1 carbon-to-nitrogen ratio; turn weekly.
  3. Choose raised beds in humid zones, sunken/zai beds in dry zones.
  4. Mulch 5â10 cm around plants; keep 5 cm clear of stems.
  5. Brew manure tea 3â7 days; dilute 1:1 before use.
  6. Never apply raw manure within 90 days of harvest on fresh-eaten herbs.
  7. Rotate herbs with legumes every 2â3 seasons.
  8. Keep input and compost records for buyer audits and cost tracking.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO Soils Portal â global soil data, fertility guides, and African soil maps
  • IITA Knowledge Center â integrated soil fertility management for African smallholders
  • KALRO (Kenya Agricultural & Livestock Research Organization) â crop-specific soil and fertilizer guides
  • CGIAR â research briefs on conservation agriculture and water harvesting in drylands
  • AGRA (Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa) â soil health and input market reports

Business takeaway: Every kilogram of compost you make on-farm replaces purchased fertilizer at 3â5Ã the cost. For a 1-acre herbal operation, that is roughly US$120â250 saved per season â money that goes straight to your margin, not your input supplier.

quiz.q: What does it mean if your soil fizzes when you add vinegar?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar reacts with alkaline soil (pH above 7) to produce fizz.

quiz.q: In a jar test, which soil particle settles first at the bottom?
quiz.explanation: Sand particles are the largest and heaviest, so they settle first.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil texture for most medicinal herbs?
quiz.explanation: Loam, with about 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay, provides good drainage and fertility.

quiz.q: How many earthworms in a 30 cm x 30 cm hole indicate healthy soil?
quiz.explanation: Finding 10 or more earthworms indicates active soil life and good fertility.

quiz.q: If your soil pH is 5.5, what should you add to raise it?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash and lime are alkaline and raise pH of acidic soil.

quiz.q: What is the ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for compost?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of about 3 parts brown (carbon) to 1 part green (nitrogen) by volume works well.

quiz.q: What temperature should a compost pile reach to kill weed seeds?
quiz.explanation: Temperatures of 55-65Â°C kill most weed seeds and pathogens.

quiz.q: Which of these should NOT be added to compost?
quiz.explanation: Meat scraps attract pests and create odors; they should not be composted.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 2 weeks aerates the pile and speeds decomposition.

quiz.q: What does it mean if your compost pile smells like rotten eggs?
quiz.explanation: A rotten egg smell indicates anaerobic conditions from too much water; add dry material and turn.

quiz.q: In a dry region, which type of bed is best?
quiz.explanation: Sunken beds catch and hold rainwater, making them ideal for dry areas.

quiz.q: How high should a raised bed be?
quiz.explanation: Raised beds are typically 20-30 cm high to improve drainage and warming.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of sunken beds?
options: D) They are easy to build
quiz.explanation: Sunken beds collect and retain water, reducing evaporation in dry climates.

quiz.q: For a 1 m x 3 m raised bed, how much soil is needed to raise it 20 cm?
quiz.explanation: Volume = 1 m x 3 m x 0.2 m = 0.6 cubic meters.

quiz.q: In a moderate climate, what type of bed is usually sufficient?
quiz.explanation: Flat beds with loosened soil and compost work well in moderate climates.

quiz.q: How thick should a mulch layer be?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of mulch effectively conserves water and suppresses weeds.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT recommended as mulch?
quiz.explanation: Fresh grass clippings mat down and rot, causing odors and disease; let them dry first.

quiz.q: How much can mulch reduce evaporation in dry regions?
quiz.explanation: A good mulch layer can reduce evaporation by 50-70%.

quiz.q: When applying mulch, how far should you keep it from the plant stem?
quiz.explanation: Leaving a 2-3 cm gap prevents rot and pest damage to the stem.

quiz.q: What is a living mulch?
options: B) Low-growing legumes planted between crops
quiz.explanation: Living mulches are plants like cowpea or groundnut that cover the soil and fix nitrogen.

quiz.q: How long should you steep manure in water to make manure tea?
quiz.explanation: Steeping for 3-7 days extracts nutrients effectively.

quiz.q: What is the correct dilution for manure tea before applying to plants?
options: A) 1 part tea to 1 part water
B) 1 part tea to 3 parts water
C) 1 part tea to 10 parts water
quiz.explanation: Diluting 1:3 with water prevents burning plants; chicken manure may need 1:5.

quiz.q: Which material is rich in potassium for liquid fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is high in potassium and also raises soil pH.

quiz.q: How often should you apply liquid fertilizer to herbs?
quiz.explanation: Applying every 2 weeks provides a steady nutrient supply without over-fertilizing.

quiz.q: What is the best time to apply foliar fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Early morning or evening reduces evaporation and leaf burn.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation important for soil health?
options: A) It prevents pest and disease buildup
quiz.explanation: Rotation disrupts pest cycles and prevents depletion of specific nutrients.

quiz.q: Which plant family is best for replenishing nitrogen in soil?
quiz.explanation: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil through symbiotic bacteria.

quiz.q: In a 4-season rotation, which should follow leafy herbs?
quiz.explanation: A typical rotation: leafy herbs, then root herbs, then legumes, then fruiting herbs.

quiz.q: What is intercropping?
options: A) Growing one crop at a time
B) Growing two or more crops together
quiz.explanation: Intercropping is growing two or more crops in the same space at the same time.

quiz.q: Which legume is drought-tolerant and good for intercropping in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Cowpea is well-adapted to dry conditions and fixes nitrogen.
